query: Consider a FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy coating on a Cu matrix under nanoindentation and friction conditions. The system is observed to have stable wear resistance and high elastic modulus at room temperature (300 K), but a sharp decline in wear resistance occurs at elevated temperatures. Given that lattice softening and atomic disorder are potential failure modes, how does the evolution of dislocation density and stacking fault structures with temperature explain the transition from stable to unstable wear behavior? Define the critical temperature threshold where the mechanism shifts from defect-mediated plasticity to rapid lattice disorder.

generation.hypothesis: In FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy coatings on Cu matrices, the transition from stable to unstable wear resistance at elevated temperatures is driven by a shift from defect-mediated plasticity (dislocation glide and climb) to rapid lattice disorder (dynamic recrystallization and atomic diffusion). At room temperature (300 K), high stacking fault energy and low dislocation mobility maintain a stable dislocation network, providing high elastic modulus and wear resistance. As temperature increases, lattice softening reduces the Peierls barrier, promoting dislocation climb and cross-slip. Above a critical threshold (~500–600°C), thermal activation triggers dynamic recrystallization and severe atomic disorder, causing a sharp decline in wear resistance due to loss of structural integrity and accelerated diffusion-controlled deformation.
generation.material_initial_state: FeNiCrCoCu high-entropy alloy coating with FCC structure, high dislocation density, and nano-sized precipitates on a Cu matrix at 300 K.
generation.intervention: Application of nanoindentation and friction under increasing temperature conditions (300 K to >600°C).
generation.conditions: Room temperature (300 K) to elevated temperatures (up to 700°C), with applied stress and frictional loading.
generation.structural_mediator: Dislocation density evolution and stacking fault energy changes, leading to dynamic recrystallization and lattice disorder.
generation.mechanism: At low temperatures, wear resistance is maintained by dislocation glide and climb controlled by lattice diffusion. At high temperatures, thermal activation promotes dynamic recrystallization and atomic disorder, reducing mechanical stability and causing rapid wear.
generation.predicted_outcome: Stable wear resistance and high elastic modulus at 300 K; sharp decline in wear resistance above ~500–600°C due to transition to rapid lattice disorder.
generation.baseline: Conventional high-entropy alloys exhibit similar temperature-dependent wear behavior, but FeNiCrCoCu shows enhanced stability at room temperature due to its specific composition.
generation.boundary: The critical temperature threshold is estimated at 500–600°C, beyond which dynamic recrystallization dominates. The mechanism is valid for FCC-structured HEAs with moderate stacking fault energy.
generation.uncertainty: The exact critical temperature may vary depending on alloy composition, processing history, and specific friction conditions. The role of the Cu matrix interface is not fully quantified.
generation.falsification_experiment: Conduct nanoindentation and friction tests on FeNiCrCoCu coatings at incremental temperatures (300 K to 800°C) while monitoring dislocation density and stacking fault structures via in-situ TEM. If wear resistance remains stable above 600°C without dynamic recrystallization, the hypothesis is falsified.

SLM-built HEA had a face-centered cubic (FCC) single-phase random solid solution. In addition, SLM-built HEA was composed of epitaxial growth grains, dislocation network and nano-sized oxides. Room- and high-temperature compression tests confirmed that SLM-built HEA has outstanding mechanical properties in all temperature ranges compared to equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi HEAs reported up to the present. The excellent mechanical properties of SLM-built HEA were achieved with fine grains, high dislocation density and fine precipitates at low temperatures (25 °C to 600 °C), and by high dislocation density and fine precipitates at high temperatures (700 °C or higher). On the other hand, the deformation microstructure showed that slip and deformation twins are the main deformation mechanisms from 25 °C to 600 °C, and slip and partial recrystallization are the main deformation mechanisms above 700 °C. The tensile creep behavior of an equiatomic CoCrFeNiMn high-entropy alloy was systematically investigated over an intermediate temperature range (500–600 °C) and applied stress (140–400 MPa). The alloy exhibited a stress-dependent transition from a low-stress region (LSR-region I) to a high-stress region (HSR-region II). The LSR was characterized by a stress exponent of 5 to 6 and an average activation energy of 268 kJ mol −1 , whereas the HSR showed much higher corresponding values of 8.9–14 and 380 kJ mol −1 . Microstructural examinations on the deformed samples revealed remarkable dynamic recrystallization at higher stress levels. Dislocation jogging and tangling configurations were frequently observed in LSR and HSR at 550 and 600 °C, respectively. Moreover, dynamic precipitates identified as M 23 C 6 or a Cr-rich σ phase were formed along grain boundaries in HSR. The diffusion-compensated strain rate versus modulus-compensated stress data analysis implied that the creep deformation in both stress regions was dominated by stress-assisted dislocation climb controlled by lattice diffusion. The observed jog configurations are indicative of a dislocation climb process, and thus the stress-assisted dislocation climb controlled by lattice diffusion may be the operative creep mechanism of the present high-entropy alloy in LSR. Contrary to LSR, creep deformation in HSR exhibits abnormally high stress exponents of 8.9–14 and an average activation energy of 380 kJ mol −1 . Combined with the dislocation configurations in Figure 8 c and Figure 9 c, the same creep mechanism may also be considered rate-controlling. The unusually high stress exponents and activation energy in several traditional alloys have been frequently described using the power-law breakdown equation [ [43] , [44] , [45] , [46] ]. However, no deviation from the linear relationship on double-logarithmic curves of log ε ˙ ~ log σ were observed, and therefore, the power-law breakdown assumption may be inappropriate for the present alloy.
